Let Bob’s three guesses be g₁, g₂, g₃.  For a particular distribution of coins (a,b,c) and a host-chosen assignment of boxes to guesses, Bob wins a total of
Σ gᵢ (only when gᵢ ≤ assigned coins).

Among the twelve possible coin multisets that satisfy the two conditions, the hardest ones for Bob are those containing a zero box, e.g. (0,6,24) and (0,12,18).  In any such distribution at most two boxes can meet any positive guess value.  

If Bob makes the same positive guess s for all three boxes, his guaranteed return is
  • 2s   for 1 ≤ s ≤ 6 (because exactly two boxes reach s in the worst cases),
  •  s   for 7 ≤ s ≤ 12 (only one box reaches s in (0,6,24)).
The maximum of these lower bounds occurs at s = 6 (or equivalently s = 12), giving a guaranteed 12 coins.  Any non-uniform choice lets the host pair the largest guess with a small or empty box, dropping the minimum below 12.

Thus the optimal strategy is to guess (6,6,6), guaranteeing 12 coins.  Each coin is worth $1,000, so the minimum money Bob can force is 12 × 1,000 = $12,000.
